claim: Collected 2026-11-18: the first pass used general-term web searches (summaries only); the second pass the same day downloaded 12 papers as PDF, converted them with pdftotext and read the text.
On the second pass rows 1, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 14, 16 and 17 were changed to QUOTED; the other rows are unchanged from the first pass.
Page numbers in this file are PDF pages; the L numbers are lines of raw pdftotext output kept in the scratchpad, not in this repository.
Each URL in the file's list of URLs tried was opened, converted with pdftotext and read, except the ones the file lists as failed.
Failed fetches: the se.cs.uni-saarland.de copies of FSE2011 and ASE2012 gave no connection (the Passau copies worked), and infosun LAS+17 returned an HTML error page, not a PDF.
The hal.inria.fr link inria-00108523 is a different paper (Oster and others 2006, WOOT); it was read and not used.

Clements and others (SOSP 2013) scalable commutativity: the paper text was read and its sentences are quoted in this file; the ACM TOCS journal version was not read.

Shapiro and others, state-based and operation-based CRDTs: the INRIA reports RR-7506 and RR-7687 were read in full and are quoted in this file.
Sequence CRDT results for Treedoc, Logoot, LSEQ and RGA are known only as search summaries, and their four references are from memory (textbook).
The Fugue paper and the interleaving anomaly (Kleppmann and others 2019; Weidner and Kleppmann 2023) are known from a search only.
Operational transformation: the counterexample results (dOPT, Imine and others, Boucheneb and Imine) are quoted from the papers; Ellis and Gibbs 1989 was not read.
Real-time editors (Jupiter, Google Wave, Google Docs, and the OT versus CRDT position paper) are known from search summaries; Etherpad, Figma, Yjs and Automerge are not verified.
The replicated tree with move operation (Kleppmann, Mulligan, Gomes and Beresford): the paper text was read in full and is quoted.
Kleppmann and Beresford's JSON CRDT (Automerge's model) is standard knowledge from memory and was not fetched.
CALM theorem (Hellerstein and Alvaro, arXiv 1901.01930): the paper text was read in full and is quoted; the Ameloot 2013 proof was not fetched.
Invariant confluence (Bailis and others, PVLDB 2014/2015): the paper text was read and is quoted; its appendices (proofs) were not read.
Eventual consistency (Vogels 2009) and session guarantees (Terry and others 1994) are from memory and were not fetched.
Bayou (Terry and others, SOSP 1995) is known from a search summary only.
Dynamo (DeCandia and others, SOSP 2007) is known from third-party summaries; the shopping cart example is from memory (textbook).
Three-way merge diff3 (Khanna, Kunal and Pierce, FSTTCS 2007): the paper text was read in full and is quoted.
Patch theory (Darcs, the categorical theory of patches, Pijul) is known from search summaries; Darcs 2005 is from memory (textbook).
Semistructured merge (Apel and others, FSE 2011) and its OOPSLA 2017 and 2019 follow-up studies: the paper texts were read and are quoted.
Structured merge with auto-tuning (Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer, ASE 2012): the paper text was read in full and is quoted; the Lessenich 2017 paper was not read.

Clements and others (SOSP 2013) scalable commutativity rule: for a history H = X||Y where Y SIM-commutes and M can generate H, a correct implementation exists whose steps in region Y are conflict-free; in plain form, whenever interface operations commute they can be implemented in a way that scales.

Clements and others: SIM commutativity is state-dependent and interface-based, and two open calls with O_CREAT|O_EXCL often do not commute (they commute when called from processes with different working directories).
Clements and others: commutativity suffices for conflict-free access but 'may not be necessary' (paper p7), and their construction is 'not very practical' (paper p4).
Clements and others: no correct implementation is conflict-free across all histories, so a designer must choose which commutative situations matter most (paper p7).

Clements and others (COMMUTER): of 13,664 generated tests, Linux scales for 68% and sv6 for 99%; sv6 is conflict-free for 13,528 tests and Linux for 9,389, so 4,275 Linux cases were not conflict-free.
Clements and others: POSIX open must allocate the lowest unused file descriptor, so such calls do not commute; sv6 adds an O_ANYFD flag to remove that constraint.
Clements and others: ScaleFS never reuses inode numbers and generates them from a per-core counter.
Clements and others, measured on 80 cores: with the commutative fstatx, statbench scales perfectly and has zero L2 cache misses.
Clements and others, on 80 cores: fstat is 3.9x more expensive than on Linux, the cost of the scalable link count.

Clements and others, mail server benchmark: non-commutative operations collapse throughput at a small number of cores, while commutative APIs reach '7.5x scalability from 1 socket (10 cores) to 8 sockets'.

Shapiro and others (INRIA RR-7506): any two replicas of a state-based CRDT eventually converge, assuming payload is transmitted infinitely often over eventually-reliable point-to-point channels (Proposition 2.1).

Shapiro and others (INRIA RR-7506): replicas of an operation-based CRDT converge under reliable broadcast delivering in delivery order, with concurrent operations commuting; causal delivery does not require consensus (Proposition 2.2).
Shapiro and others (RR-7506, paper p41): 'CRDTs tend to become inefficient over time, as tombstones accumulate and internal data structures become unbalanced'.
Shapiro and others (RR-7506, paper p42): removing tombstones, rebalancing Treedoc or resetting a 2P-Set payload needs atomic unanimous agreement such as 2-Phase Commit or Paxos Commit.
Shapiro and others (RR-7506, paper p20): a non-negative counter invariant cannot be evaluated on local information, so two replicas at value 1 that both decrement converge to -1.
Shapiro and others (RR-7506, paper p19): decrementing a max-merge counter would violate monotonicity.
Shapiro, Preguica, Baquero and Zawirski (SSS 2011, RR-7687): replicas of any CRDT converge in a self-stabilising manner despite any number of failures.
SSS 2011 Theorem 2.1 (RR-7687): assuming eventual delivery and termination, any state-based object satisfying the monotonic semilattice property is SEC (strong eventual consistency).
SSS 2011 Theorem 2.2 (RR-7687): assuming causal delivery of updates and method termination, any op-based object satisfying the commutativity property for all concurrent updates is SEC.
SSS 2011 (RR-7687) calls the two conditions 'a strong equivalence' (paper p6) and says 'SEC is weaker than strong consistency' (paper p12).
Treedoc (Preguica and others 2009, summary): its best case is a plain array, and its authors report reasonable costs on real editing traces (figure not recalled).
LSEQ slides (Nedelec and others 2013, summary): a document with 1 million operations ending at 1 line can hold 499,999 tombstones.
A 2026 preprint (no author named in the file) says LSEQ still shows unbounded identifier growth under intense editing; a qualitative claim.
Kleppmann and others named the interleaving anomaly: Logoot and LSEQ show it, and RGA avoids the main form (mechanised proof) but has a milder one.
The Fugue paper (Weidner and Kleppmann, arXiv 2305.00583, summary) reports that almost all surveyed CRDT and OT text algorithms suffer from interleaving.

The errata page of Kleppmann and others' PaPoC 2019 paper says its non-interleaving definition (section 2.1) cannot be met by any algorithm, and its algorithm (section 3.1) does not guarantee convergence.

Cormack (Waterloo CS-95-08): dOPT is shown by counterexample to be incorrect; a corrected algorithm exists for point-to-point communication, and there appears to be no simple correction for broadcast.
Imine, Molli, Oster and Rusinowitch (ECSCW 2003): transformation functions must satisfy C1 (same state in either order) and C2 (transforming against a sequence does not depend on the order).

Imine and others (ECSCW 2003): published string transformation functions are not correct; the prover found a C1 counterexample 'in a few seconds', and further functions violate C2 with three concurrent operations.
Imine and others (ECSCW 2003) call Suleiman's transformation functions 'over-specified'.

Boucheneb and Imine (INRIA RR-6510, 2008, model checking): with more than 2 sites, convergence fails for all five IT algorithms they considered, with a counterexample for each; this covers their chosen algorithms, not all published ones.
Jupiter (Nichols and others, UIST 1995, summary): one central server, each client talks only to the server, and the server fixes a total order; one source also says Google Docs uses OT (secondary).

Sun and others (arXiv 1810.02137 and companions, 2018-2019, summary) argue CRDT text solutions also follow a transformation approach and OT is still the choice in most production co-editors; the file calls it an authors' position paper, not a neutral benchmark.

Kleppmann, Mulligan, Gomes and Beresford (IEEE TPDS): the move-operation algorithm 'requires no synchronous coordination between replicas', and the paper demonstrates bugs in Google Drive and Dropbox with concurrent moves.
Kleppmann and others (move operation): Isabelle-proved theorems cover a unique parent, no cycles, convergence and strong eventual consistency.
Kleppmann and others (move operation): when two operations would introduce a cycle, the one with the greater timestamp is ignored, so a move can be silently dropped.
Kleppmann and others (move operation): replicas can each perform operations that are individually safe but whose combination leads to a cycle, so local checks are not enough.

Kleppmann and others (move operation; three replicas in California, Ireland and Singapore): state machine replication has approximately four times higher throughput than their algorithm, but their algorithm has up to 100,000 times lower latency.

Kleppmann and others (move operation, paper p10): the leader-based baseline ran 14,000 move operations per second against the CRDT's 600 with Isabelle-generated code, and 22,000 against 5,700 with hand-written code.
Kleppmann and others (move operation): local CRDT operations take '1-2 µs' and a leader round trip takes 145-176 ms.
Kleppmann and others (move operation): at peak there are '200 undos and redos per remote operation'.

Kleppmann and others (move operation): the algorithm keeps operations in its log indefinitely, so memory grows without bound; truncation needs causal stability with a known replica set and FIFO links.
Kleppmann and others (move operation): deletion has no fast path and must go through the undo-do-redo process.
Hellerstein and Alvaro, 'Keeping CALM' (arXiv 1901.01930), Theorem 1: a program has a consistent, coordination-free distributed implementation if and only if it is monotonic.
Hellerstein and Alvaro (CALM): a program P is monotonic if for any input sets S and T with S a subset of T, P(S) is a subset of P(T).
Hellerstein and Alvaro (CALM): non-monotonic programs cannot proceed until they know all information has arrived, so they must coordinate.
Hellerstein and Alvaro (CALM): deadlock detection needs no coordination because its decisions are stable, while garbage collection does, because its decisions can be invalidated by new information.

Hellerstein and Alvaro (CALM, shopping cart): additions and deletions kept as two growing sets commute, but neither commutes with checkout, so shopping is coordination-free while checkout still needs coordination.

Hellerstein and Alvaro (CALM, paper p1): state-of-the-art multiprocessor key-value stores can spend 90% of their time waiting for coordination, and the coordination-free Anna ran over two orders of magnitude faster.
Hellerstein and Alvaro (CALM): bare assignment is a nonmonotonic construct, which makes the CALM theorem extremely hard to apply to imperative programs.
Bailis and others (PVLDB 8(3)): the I-confluence property ensures that divergent but I-valid database states can be merged into a valid database state.

Bailis and others (I-confluence theorem): a globally I-valid system can execute transactions with coordination-freedom, transactional availability and convergence if and only if they are I-confluent with respect to the invariant I.

Bailis and others (TPC-C workload): ten of twelve TPC-C invariants are I-confluent under the workload transactions, and coordination-free execution reached over 12.7M TPC-C New-Order transactions per second on 200 servers, a 25-fold improvement over prior results.
Bailis and others (TPC-C): two invariants are not I-confluent with the workload transactions and need coordination; per district, order IDs should be assigned sequentially.

Bailis and others, Table 2, I-confluent (yes) rows: attribute equality and inequality, uniqueness when the system chooses the value, foreign key insert, cascading delete, secondary index update, materialized view update, counter increment under '>' and decrement under '<', and NOT CONTAINS on sets, lists and maps.

Bailis and others, Table 2, not I-confluent (no) rows: uniqueness when the user chooses the value, AUTO_INCREMENT insert, foreign key delete, counter decrement under '>' and increment under '<', and SIZE= on sets, lists and maps.
Bailis and others: uniqueness is not I-confluent for inserts of unique values, but it can be achieved without coordination as long as there is a notion of replica membership.
Bailis and others: a '>' threshold invariant is I-confluent for counter increment and assign but not for decrement, so concurrent salary increments are safe and concurrent salary decrements are not.
Bailis and others: arbitrary deletion of records is unsafe for foreign keys, since a user might be added to a department that was concurrently deleted.
Bailis and others: of the 14 non-TPC-C OLTP-Bench workloads, nine did not involve integrity constraints, one matched TPC-C, two needed unique ID assignment and two were research benchmarks.

Bailis and others (microbenchmark): coordination-free execution exceeded 12M transactions per second, the lock-based version about 1.1M, and for distributed transactions locking throughput dropped by over three orders of magnitude.
Bailis and others: if invariants are incorrectly or incompletely specified, an I-confluent database system may violate application-level correctness.
Vogels 2009 (eventual consistency, textbook, not fetched): if updates stop, replicas converge.
Eventual consistency gives convergence only after quiescence and says nothing about whether the converged value is right (textbook, file's guarantee note).
Session guarantees (read your writes, monotonic reads, writes follow reads, monotonic writes) are from Terry and others, PDIS 1994 (textbook, not fetched).
Last-writer-wins silently drops a concurrent write (textbook, not fetched).

Bayou (Terry and others, SOSP 1995, summary): each write carries a dependency check and a merge procedure, which runs when the check fails at a replica and may rewrite the write or leave it for a person.
Bayou (summary): replicas that apply the same writes in the same order reach the same state; no bound on this was recalled.

Dynamo (DeCandia and others, SOSP 2007, summary, partly third-party): a sloppy quorum takes the first healthy nodes on the ring, vector clocks tag versions, and when neither version dominates the client merges them (shopping cart: union).
Dynamo latency figures are not confirmed against the paper: secondary sources give about 200 ms and sub-300 ms at the 99.9th percentile, and they disagree.
Deleted items can reappear after a union merge in Dynamo's shopping cart example (textbook, from the paper's example).
Dynamo's sloppy quorum loses the read-write overlap guarantee (summary).

Khanna, Kunal and Pierce (diff3, FSTTCS 2007): every safe tiling-respecting configuration (A O B) leads to a unique conflict-free synchronization, where safe means the O2 component contains an element x occurring exactly once in each of O, A and B.

Khanna, Kunal and Pierce (diff3): the two obvious separation conditions (a long untouched middle; a middle occurring nowhere else) are each not enough, and the generalisation to several edited regions no longer ensures a conflict-free synchronization.
Khanna, Kunal and Pierce (diff3): diff3 is not idempotent, does not guarantee near success on similar replicas, and is not stable even for non-conflicting runs.

Apel and others (FSE 2011, semistructured merge with conflict handlers): on 180 sample merge scenarios, conflicts fall in 60 % of scenarios by 34±21 %, conflicting lines fall in 82% by 61±22 %, and conflicting files fall in 72 % by 28±12 %.
Apel and others (FSE 2011): semistructured merge increases the number of conflicts in 26 percent (46 of 180) of scenarios, by 109±170 %.
Apel and others (FSE 2011): semistructured merge struggles with renames because superimposition relies on nominal equality, and its revisions must be syntactically correct.
Apel and others (FSE 2011): combining unstructured and semistructured merge reduces conflicts by a further 35 % compared with pure unstructured merge.
Cavalcanti, Borba, Seibt and Apel (2019 study of 43,509 scenarios from 508 Java projects): semistructured and structured merge differ in 24% of the scenarios with conflicts.
Cavalcanti and others (2019 study): overall the two merges differ in 0.58 percent (253) of all scenarios; scenarios with conflicts are 1,007 against 814, and conflicts found are 4,732 and 4,793.
Cavalcanti and others (2019 study): false positives occur in 36 scenarios for semistructured and 4 for structured merge; false negatives occur in 39 for structured and 5 for semistructured.
Cavalcanti and others (2019 study): the paper does not have the ground truth, so false positives and negatives are judged from Travis CI builds, tests and manual reading.
Cavalcanti and others (2019 study): the two merges differ when changes occur in overlapping text areas that correspond to different AST nodes.
Cavalcanti, Borba and Accioly (OOPSLA 2017; 34,030 scenarios from 50 Java projects): 19,238 conflicts with unstructured merge and 14,544 with semistructured merge, a reduction of approximately 24%.

Cavalcanti, Borba and Accioly (OOPSLA 2017): additional false positives are 43.47 ± 19.01 % of unstructured conflicts and 30.21 ± 20.68 % of semistructured conflicts; additional false negatives are 20.60 ± 21.30 % for semistructured and 9.62 ± 16.29 % for unstructured, an upper bound the file calls overestimated.
Cavalcanti, Borba and Accioly (OOPSLA 2017, paper p3): 'we find no evidence that semistructured merge leads to fewer false negatives'.
Improved tool s3m (cited in the OOPSLA 2017 entry, paper p18): it reduces the number of reported conflicts by half, adds no false positives, and has at least 8% fewer false negatives.

Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer (ASE 2012): structured merge with auto-tuning is up to 12 times faster than purely structured merge and 5 times on average, on 8 Java projects with 72 merge scenarios and over 17 million lines of code.
Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer (ASE 2012): on average structured merge reports 39 % of the conflicts and 24 % of the conflicting lines of unstructured merge, mostly ordering conflicts.
Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer (ASE 2012): auto-tuning misses few conflicts, up to 26 (in FreeCol) and 2 on average.
Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer (ASE 2012): unstructured merge is up to 71 times faster than structured merge, and 15 times faster on average.
Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer (ASE 2012): 21 % of changed files cannot be merged with unstructured merge, twice the fraction Mens predicted, and structured merge reduces that to 15 %.

Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer (ASE 2012): auto-tuning is less precise than a purely structured merge, and tree matching of largest common subtrees considers only corresponding tree levels, so shifted code is not matched.
Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer (ASE 2012): structured approaches have at least cubic or even exponential time complexity.
Darcs (Roundy 2005, textbook, figure not recalled): Darcs had exponential-time merge cases.
Patch theory (textbook): when a merge of two patches with a common source exists it is unique up to isomorphism, and it is independent of order.

Mimram and Di Giusto (arXiv 1311.3903, 2013, summary): files are objects and patches morphisms; a merge is a pushout, which need not exist when patches conflict, so the category is extended so conflicts become first-class objects.
Darcs (summary): patches commute when order does not matter, and conflicts were to be handled by extra constructs named mergers, conflictors and graphictors, which were proposals.

Commutativity (Clements and others): wins where the interface can be changed so operations commute, and loses where the interface is fixed and its operations do not commute, since the rule then says nothing.
note: The file gives this as its wins/loses reading; it is not tested here.

claim: Commutativity-based concurrency control (Weihl): wins for types with rich operations such as counters, sets and queues where read/write locking blocks needlessly; loses where operations that do not commute still block or abort.
note: The file gives this as its wins/loses reading; it is not tested here.

claim: CRDTs (Shapiro and others): win on availability, offline work and no central server; lose where a data type's invariant needs agreement, and metadata can grow.
note: The file gives this as its wins/loses reading; it is not tested here.

claim: Sequence CRDTs for text: win on character-level concurrent editing without a server; lose on memory and identifier growth, and history needs compaction, which itself needs coordination.
note: The file gives this as its wins/loses reading; it is not tested here.

claim: Operational transformation: wins on compact documents, no tombstones and intent-preserving rich operations; loses because transformation functions are hard to get right and many published algorithms were later found faulty.
note: The file gives this as its wins/loses reading; it is not tested here.

claim: CALM theorem: wins as a design test applied to a program, not a data type; loses because monotonicity is a strong test and says 'needs coordination', not how cheap coordination can be.
note: The file gives this as its wins/loses reading; it is not tested here.

claim: Invariant confluence: wins for foreign-key inserts, replica-generated unique ids, counters moving the safe way and derived views; loses for chosen-value uniqueness, sequential ids, deletes others depend on, and thresholds crossed in the unsafe direction.
note: The file gives this as its wins/loses reading; it is not tested here.

claim: Bayou: wins on semantic conflicts that a generic rule cannot settle; loses because the application author writes merge code per operation.
note: The file gives this as its wins/loses reading; it is not tested here.

claim: diff3: wins on line-based text with edits in different places; loses on moved or reordered text, adjacent edits, and any edit whose meaning depends on code elsewhere.
note: The file gives this as its wins/loses reading; it is not tested here.

claim: Across the schemes: each names a condition on operations (commute, monotone, invariant-confluent, transformable) or hands residual conflicts to code or a person; where the condition fails, each falls back on a server's ordering, application merge code or a reported conflict.
note: The file's reading aid, headed 'no mapping to our case, no verdict'; it is not tested here.
